name: Serverfarm

profile.address: 840, South Canal Street, Near West Side, Chicago, West Chicago Township, Cook County, Illinois, 60607
profile.reading:
Serverfarm's CH1 data center occupies an eight story building at 840 South Canal Street in Chicago's Near West Side, close to Union Station and the Kennedy Expressway. Serverfarm is a data center developer and operator whose origins trace to Red Sea Group's 1999 entry into the data center business with a facility in Dallas, and which expanded over the following two decades by acquiring and repositioning existing buildings in markets including Santa Clara, San Jose, Toronto, Atlanta, London, Amsterdam, and Chicago, rebranding from Server Farm Realty to Serverfarm in 2016. In 2023, Manulife Investment Management agreed to acquire a controlling interest in the company, a transaction Serverfarm's own materials describe as a significant shift in its ownership structure.

According to Serverfarm's own facility page, CH1 totals about 443,000 square feet across its eight floors, of which roughly 130,000 square feet is colocation hall space. The building draws 32 megawatts of utility power and offers 21.5 megawatts of IT capacity to tenants, delivered over twelve diverse power feeds fed from four separate electrical substations, a level of feed diversity aimed at protecting tenants from single points of failure upstream of the building. Cooling runs through a central water cooled chiller plant with waterside economizers, and Serverfarm states an average power usage effectiveness of 1.4 for the facility.

On connectivity, Serverfarm advertises access to thirteen telecommunications carriers, including Zayo, XO, Level 3, AT&T, and Verizon, through two meet me rooms, plus direct cloud on ramps to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. The company also highlights direct access to two long haul fiber network conduits that run roughly 55 feet beneath Canal Street, a detail tied to the building's position along a historic Chicago telecommunications duct corridor.

Serverfarm's public materials do not state the building's original construction date, its use prior to becoming a data center, or the identity of current tenants, so that history is not part of the public record as published by the operator. What is documented is a large, heavily powered, carrier dense colocation facility that fits squarely within Serverfarm's stated strategy of acquiring and modernizing existing large footprint buildings in major metros rather than building new ones from the ground up.

profile.business_description: Global data center developer and operator focused on AI-ready, build-to-suit, high-density data centers

reading:
Serverfarm describes itself as a global data centre developer and operator with more than 25 years of operating experience, focused on high density build to suit space aimed at AI workloads. Its distinguishing habit is that it buys and rebuilds existing buildings rather than starting on green fields, which puts it in a small group within this registry. That approach shapes what can be known about it. Serverfarm does not publish a headquarters address, an exact founding year, or an ownership structure on its own site, and the registry records those as not published rather than estimating them. It lists nine operational North American locations, Clarksville, Atlanta, Chicago, two in Houston, Los Angeles, Northern Virginia, Moses Lake in Washington and Toronto, plus Amsterdam, London and two sites in Israel, with further sites described as coming.

The registry holds two Serverfarm facilities, one in Illinois and one in California. The Illinois site is CH1 at 840 South Canal Street in Chicago, an eight storey building of about 443,000 square feet with roughly 130,000 square feet of data hall. CH1 is one of the clearest published examples in this registry of the difference between the two power numbers that get conflated most often. Serverfarm states 32 megawatts of utility power reaching the building over twelve diverse feeds from four separate substations, and separately states 21.5 megawatts of critical IT load. Any directory listing that reports a single capacity number for CH1 is almost certainly reporting the 32 megawatt utility figure and calling it capacity. The building runs at about 150 watts per square foot with a stated power usage effectiveness around 1.4, cooled by a central water cooled chiller plant with waterside economisers. Its connectivity is a function of the address rather than the equipment, with thirteen network providers on site, cloud on ramps to the major platforms, and direct access to two long haul fibre tunnel ducts running about 55 feet beneath Canal Street.

The California row is less settled. Serverfarm's own press release and trade coverage record its purchase of a 12 megawatt Los Angeles data centre in El Segundo from T5 Data Centers, an operator separately profiled in this registry, for approximately 71 million dollars. That is a documented transfer between two operators already in this dataset. Whether the registry's California row is that same El Segundo building has not been confirmed here, and this entry does not assert it. If facility level research confirms the match, the correct treatment is to record T5 as a former operator of that site rather than to treat it as a Serverfarm build. Serverfarm publishes no capacity figure for a California site on its own pages, and the 12 megawatt number attached to the El Segundo transaction describes the asset as reported at the time of sale rather than a current specification. No municipal or utility docket covering either the Chicago or the El Segundo building surfaced in this research, which is unsurprising, because both are conversions of existing buildings already connected to the grid and therefore rarely generate the rezoning or siting record that a new campus does.
